structure.rationale: The request arrived as a five-chapter outline (why it exists, the mental model, the flows, security, building). That order is right — problem, model, mechanics, hazards, practice — so it is kept intact as five chapters. Two chapters are added where the outline pointed at material it had no room for: a token-anatomy chapter after the mental model (the outline's chapter 2 names access tokens, refresh tokens and scopes but the details of opaque-vs-JWT, audience and introspection belong together in one place, and chapters 4-6 all depend on them), and a closing chapter on OpenID Connect and OAuth 2.1, which the outline listed only as a final bullet despite being the thing most readers meet next. Every chapter is grounded in the RFC that normatively defines the behavior rather than in secondary write-ups.
structure.audience: Working developers who have used a 'Sign in with…' button or integrated a third-party API, and now need to reason about, choose, and debug OAuth flows themselves.

claims.text: OAuth 2.0 defines exactly four roles: resource owner, resource server, client, and authorization server.
The resource owner is an entity capable of granting access to a protected resource; when the resource owner is a person, it is referred to as an end-user.
The resource server is the server hosting the protected resources, capable of accepting and responding to protected resource requests using access tokens.
The client is an application making protected resource requests on behalf of the resource owner and with its authorization.
The authorization server is the server issuing access tokens to the client after successfully authenticating the resource owner and obtaining authorization.
The client is issued a different set of credentials than those of the resource owner, and uses an access token rather than the resource owner's credentials to access protected resources.
An access token is a string denoting a specific scope, lifetime, and other access attributes.

A web application is a confidential client running on a web server, where client credentials and issued access tokens are stored on the server and are not exposed to or accessible by the resource owner.

A user-agent-based application is a public client whose code is downloaded from a web server and executes within a user-agent, where protocol data and credentials are easily accessible and often visible to the resource owner.
If the client type is confidential, or the client was issued client credentials or assigned other authentication requirements, the client MUST authenticate with the authorization server.
The authorization server MUST require the use of TLS for requests to both the authorization endpoint and the token endpoint.
GitHub's authorization endpoint is https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize and the authorization code is exchanged by POSTing to https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token.

pitfalls: Conflating the roles: the same company often runs both the authorization server and the resource server, which hides the fact that they are separate responsibilities with separate trust boundaries.
Treating OAuth as a login protocol. OAuth 2.0 grants delegated access to resources; proving who the user is requires OpenID Connect on top of it.
Assuming a 'client' means a browser or a phone. In OAuth the client is the application requesting access — it may well be a server.

claims.text: The authorization endpoint is used by the authorization code and implicit grant flows; the client signals the desired grant using the response_type parameter, whose value is 'code' for an authorization code or 'token' for an access token.

The token endpoint is used by the client to obtain an access token by presenting its authorization grant or refresh token, and is used with every authorization grant except the implicit grant, where the token is issued directly from the authorization endpoint.
In the authorization request, the client adds parameters to the query component of the authorization endpoint URI using application/x-www-form-urlencoded format.
In the authorization request, response_type is REQUIRED and its value MUST be set to 'code' for the authorization code grant; client_id is REQUIRED; redirect_uri and scope are OPTIONAL.

In the authorization request, state is RECOMMENDED — an opaque value used by the client to maintain state between the request and callback, which the authorization server includes when redirecting the user-agent back to the client.
In the access token request the client sends grant_type with the value 'authorization_code', plus code, redirect_uri, and client_id, to the token endpoint.
The client includes the redirection URI used to obtain the authorization code in the token request for verification purposes.
If the access token request is valid and authorized, the authorization server issues an access token and an optional refresh token.
Using the authorization server as an intermediary to obtain the authorization grant — rather than having the client collect the resource owner's credentials — is the preferred method.
A maximum authorization code lifetime of 10 minutes is RECOMMENDED, and the client MUST NOT use the authorization code more than once.
If an authorization code is used more than once, the authorization server MUST deny the request and SHOULD revoke, when possible, all tokens previously issued based on that authorization code.

Refresh tokens are credentials used to obtain access tokens: they are issued to the client by the authorization server and used to obtain a new access token when the current one becomes invalid or expires, or to obtain additional access tokens with identical or narrower scope.
Client authentication requirements for the refresh request are based on the client type and on authorization server policies.

snippets.note: Authorization request; parameter names verified against RFC 6749 (line-wrapped here for reading).
Authorization response: the code comes back on the redirect, not the token.

snippets.code:
POST /token HTTP/1.1
Host: server.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=authorization_code&code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fclient.example.org%2Fcb&client_id=s6BhdRkqt3
snippets.note: Token request; parameter names verified against RFC 6749.
Token endpoint response field names per RFC 6749 §5.1; access_token and token_type are the always-present pair.

pitfalls: state is only RECOMMENDED by RFC 6749, so the base spec does not force CSRF protection — treat it as mandatory anyway.
redirect_uri is OPTIONAL in the authorization request but must be repeated in the token request whenever it was sent; a mismatch surfaces as invalid_grant, not invalid_request.
The redirect carries a code, not a token — a design people miss, and the reason a leaked redirect URL is survivable.
Authorization codes are single-use and short-lived; a retry loop that replays the same code will get invalid_grant and can revoke the tokens already issued from it.

claims.text: Clients SHOULD make authenticated requests with a bearer token using the Authorization request header field with the 'Bearer' HTTP authorization scheme.
The Bearer credentials grammar is credentials = "Bearer" 1*SP b64token, where b64token = 1*( ALPHA / DIGIT / "-" / "." / "_" / "~" / "+" / "/" ) *"=".
All challenges defined by RFC 6750 MUST use the auth-scheme value 'Bearer' in the WWW-Authenticate header field.
The invalid_token error code indicates the access token provided is expired, revoked, malformed, or invalid for other reasons, and the resource server SHOULD respond with HTTP 401 (Unauthorized).

The insufficient_scope error code indicates the request requires higher privileges than provided by the access token; the resource server SHOULD respond with HTTP 403 (Forbidden) and MAY include the 'scope' attribute naming the scope necessary to access the protected resource.
If the request lacks any authentication information, the resource server SHOULD NOT include an error code or other error information in the response.
RFC 6750 defines the error codes invalid_request, invalid_token, and insufficient_scope, and the challenge attributes realm, scope, error, error_description, and error_uri.
RFC 9068 defines a profile for issuing OAuth 2.0 access tokens in JWT format so that authorization servers and resource servers from different vendors can interoperate.
RFC 9068 registers the media type 'application/at+jwt' for an access token in JWT format, and the 'typ' header value used SHOULD be 'at+jwt'.
JWT access tokens MUST be signed; any signing algorithm may be used, but asymmetric cryptography is RECOMMENDED because it simplifies acquiring validation information for resource servers.
The resource server MUST validate the signature of all incoming JWT access tokens using the algorithm specified in the JWT 'alg' header parameter.
The authorization server's issuer identifier MUST exactly match the value of the 'iss' claim.
The resource server MUST validate that 'aud' contains a resource indicator value corresponding to an identifier it expects for itself, and MUST reject the token if it does not.
The current time MUST be before the time represented by the 'exp' claim.

Where a resource owner is involved, 'sub' SHOULD correspond to the subject identifier of the resource owner; where none is involved, such as the client credentials grant, 'sub' SHOULD correspond to an identifier for the client application.

The introspection endpoint takes a parameter representing an OAuth 2.0 token and returns a JSON document describing the meta information surrounding the token, including whether the token is currently active.
The introspection response is application/json; 'active' is the only REQUIRED member and is a boolean indicator of whether the presented token is currently active.
A true value for 'active' generally indicates the token was issued by this authorization server, has not been revoked by the resource owner, and is within its validity window.
In the introspection response, 'scope' is OPTIONAL and is a JSON string containing a space-separated list of scopes, and 'client_id' is OPTIONAL.
RFC 7009 defines an additional endpoint allowing clients to notify the authorization server that a previously obtained refresh or access token is no longer needed.

The revocation request uses application/x-www-form-urlencoded with a REQUIRED 'token' parameter and an OPTIONAL 'token_type_hint' parameter; the specification defines two hint values, access_token and refresh_token.
The 'resource' parameter value identifies a resource the client is requesting access to, and can carry the location of a protected resource, typically as an https URL or a more abstract identifier.
The resource parameter value MUST be an absolute URI and MUST NOT include a fragment component; it SHOULD NOT include a query component.

When used on an access token request at the token endpoint, for all grant types, the resource parameter indicates the target service or protected resource where the client intends to use the requested access token.
The authorization server MAY require clients to specify the resources they intend to access and MAY fail requests that omit the parameter with an invalid_target error.

Authorization server metadata is published at a '.well-known' location derived from the issuer identifier, and the default well-known URI string '/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server' is the right choice for general-purpose OAuth authorization servers.

The 'issuer' metadata field is REQUIRED and is a URL using the https scheme with no query or fragment components; 'authorization_endpoint' is REQUIRED unless no grant types are supported that use the authorization endpoint, and 'response_types_supported' is REQUIRED.
The jwks_uri references a document containing the signing key(s) the client uses to validate signatures from the authorization server, and that URL MUST use the https scheme.
The returned 'issuer' value MUST be identical to the issuer identifier into which the well-known URI string was inserted; if they are not identical, the data in the response MUST NOT be used.
If the issuer identifier contains a path component, any terminating '/' MUST be removed before inserting '/.well-known/' between the host component and the path component.
Authorization servers SHOULD use OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server Metadata to advertise their signing keys via 'jwks_uri' and the expected 'iss' value via the 'issuer' metadata value.

snippets.code:
GET /calendar/v3/events HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Bearer mF_9.B5f-4.1JqM
snippets.note: The Authorization request header form clients SHOULD use.

snippets.code:
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="example",
                  error="invalid_token",
                  error_description="The access token expired"
snippets.note: Bearer challenge for an expired token; attribute and error-code names per RFC 6750.

snippets.code:
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="example",
                  error="insufficient_scope",
                  scope="calendar.write"
snippets.note: insufficient_scope maps to 403 and MAY carry the scope required.
Introspection request; the response is application/json with a REQUIRED boolean 'active'.
Introspection response; only 'active' is required, the rest are optional metadata.
Revocation request using the REQUIRED token and OPTIONAL token_type_hint parameters.
Metadata request when the issuer identifier is https://example.com — quoted from RFC 8414.
Metadata request when the issuer identifier is https://example.com/issuer1 — the path moves after the suffix.

pitfalls: invalid_token is 401 and insufficient_scope is 403; collapsing both into 401 breaks clients that distinguish 'refresh my token' from 'ask for more scope'.
When a request carries no authentication information at all, RFC 6750 says do NOT emit an error code in the challenge.
Passing access tokens as URI query parameters leaks them into logs, Referer headers, and browser history; use the Authorization header.
Validating iss and the signature but not aud lets a token minted for one resource server be replayed against another; RFC 9068 makes the audience check mandatory.
Accepting the alg header without pinning expected algorithms (or accepting 'none') defeats signature validation entirely.
The issuer in a metadata document MUST byte-match the issuer you derived the URL from; if it does not, discard the document.
For issuers with a path component the well-known suffix goes before the path, which is the opposite of what most implementers assume.
/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server (RFC 8414) and /.well-known/openid-configuration (OpenID Connect) are distinct endpoints and may return different documents on the same host.
A JWT access token is readable by anyone who holds it — base64url is not encryption, so never put anything in it the client should not see.

claims.text: RFC 6749 defines four grant types — authorization code, implicit, resource owner password credentials, and client credentials — plus an extensibility mechanism for defining additional types.
PKCE is an extension to the authorization code flow that prevents authorization code interception, CSRF, and authorization code injection attacks.
PKCE defines two code challenge methods: 'plain' and 'S256'.
For the plain method code_challenge = code_verifier; for S256, code_challenge = BASE64URL-ENCODE(SHA256(ASCII(code_verifier))).
The code verifier ABNF is 43*128unreserved, where unreserved = ALPHA / DIGIT / '-' / '.' / '_' / '~' — i.e. 43 to 128 characters from that set.
The code verifier must be cryptographically random with high entropy so it is not practical for an attacker to guess; the client SHOULD create a code_verifier with a minimum of 256 bits of entropy.
Base64url-encoding a 32-octet random sequence produces a 43-octet URL-safe string suitable for use as the code verifier.

The S256 method protects against eavesdroppers observing or intercepting the code_challenge, because the challenge cannot be used without the verifier; servers that support PKCE are required to support S256.
When issuing the authorization code the server MUST associate the code_challenge and code_challenge_method values with that authorization code.

At the token endpoint the server transforms the received code_verifier according to the recorded code_challenge_method and compares it to the stored code_challenge; if the values are not equal the request must be rejected with an error.

If the server requires PKCE and the client does not send code_challenge, the authorization endpoint MUST return an authorization error response with error set to 'invalid_request', explaining that a code challenge is required.
Authorization servers MUST support PKCE, and public clients MUST use PKCE to prevent injection (replay) of authorization codes into the authorization response.
PKCE ensures that an attacker cannot redeem a stolen authorization code at the token endpoint without knowledge of the code_verifier.

The client credentials grant can be used when the authorization scope is limited to protected resources under the control of the client, or to protected resources previously arranged with the authorization server, and is used typically when the client is acting on its own behalf.
The device authorization response contains device_code, user_code, verification_uri, verification_uri_complete, expires_in, and interval.

verification_uri is the URI the user navigates to and supplies the user_code during interaction; verification_uri_complete is a verification URI that already includes the user_code, designed for non-textual transmission such as a QR code.
interval is the minimum time in seconds the client SHOULD wait between polling requests to the token endpoint; if no value is provided clients MUST use 5 seconds as the default.
The device access token request uses grant_type 'urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code', advertised in grant_types_supported.
authorization_pending means the authorization request is still pending and the client MUST wait at least the number of seconds specified by interval, or 5 seconds if none was provided.
slow_down is a variant of authorization_pending: polling should continue, but the interval MUST be increased by 5 seconds for this and all subsequent requests.
expired_token means the device_code has expired and the device authorization session has concluded; access_denied indicates the authorization request was denied.
Because the user code is typed by a human, shorter codes are preferred for usability, entropy is typically lower than for device codes, and the server should rate-limit user code attempts.

For user codes using only A-Z characters the user's input should be uppercased before comparison, and stripping characters outside the chosen character set reduces failures from errantly typed characters.
device_authorization_endpoint is an authorization server metadata parameter giving the URL of the device authorization endpoint.

The implicit grant (response_type=token) and other response types causing the authorization server to issue access tokens in the authorization response are vulnerable to access token leakage and access token replay.

Clients SHOULD NOT use the implicit grant or other response types issuing access tokens in the authorization response, unless access token injection is prevented and the leakage vectors are mitigated.
Clients SHOULD instead use the response type 'code', which allows the authorization server to detect replay attempts and reduces attack surface since access tokens are not exposed in URLs.
The resource owner password credentials grant MUST NOT be used.
In OAuth 2.1 the implicit grant (response_type=token) is omitted from the specification, and the resource owner password credentials grant is omitted from the specification.

Google's device flow posts to https://oauth2.googleapis.com/device/code, and that URL should be retrieved from the discovery document using the device_authorization_endpoint metadata value; the polled token endpoint is https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token.
GitHub supports the authorization code grant and the device authorization grant, with users entering the user verification code at https://github.com/login/device.

GitHub's redirect_uri parameter is optional; if omitted GitHub redirects to the callback URL configured in the OAuth app settings, and if provided the redirect URL's host (excluding sub-domains) and port must exactly match the configured callback URL.

snippets.note: The S256 transformation, quoted from RFC 7636.

snippets.code:
import os, hashlib, base64

verifier = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(os.urandom(32)).rstrip(b'=').decode('ascii')
challenge = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(
    hashlib.sha256(verifier.encode('ascii')).digest()
).rstrip(b'=').decode('ascii')
snippets.note: S256 derivation; 32 random octets yield a 43-character verifier. Executed during research and confirmed to reproduce the RFC 7636 Appendix B test vector.
RFC 7636 Appendix B test vector; independently recomputed in Python and Node during research.

snippets.code:
POST /token HTTP/1.1
Host: server.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=authorization_code&code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fclient.example.org%2Fcb&client_id=s6BhdRkqt3&code_verifier=dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk
snippets.note: Authorization code + PKCE token request; parameter names per RFC 6749 and RFC 7636.
Device grant polling request using the grant_type URN from RFC 8628.
Device flow poll response (HTTP 400) meaning the client must keep waiting at least `interval` seconds.

snippets.code:
POST /token HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Authorization: Basic czZCaGRSa3F0Mzo3RmpmcDBaQnIxS3REUmJuZlZkbUl3

grant_type=client_credentials&scope=reports.read
snippets.note: Client credentials grant: no user, no redirect, client authenticates directly.

pitfalls: Hash the ASCII bytes of the verifier string itself, never the raw random octets you generated it from — the single most common PKCE implementation bug.
The 43-128 character bound applies to the string form; deriving a verifier from 32 random characters rather than 32 random octets gives materially less entropy than the recommended 256 bits.
base64url output must have '=' padding stripped and '+'/'/' translated to '-'/'_'; leaving padding in produces a challenge the server will reject.
A server that silently accepts code_challenge_method=plain, or ignores a missing code_challenge, provides no protection at all.
slow_down requires increasing the interval by 5 seconds for that and all subsequent requests; a client that resets to the original interval will be throttled or cut off.
If interval is absent the device client MUST default to 5 seconds; defaulting to 0 or 1 produces a tight polling loop.
authorization_pending and slow_down are normal flow control, not failures — only expired_token and access_denied terminate the poll.
'Discouraged' understates the implicit grant's status: RFC 9700 says clients SHOULD NOT use it, and OAuth 2.1 omits it entirely.
The password grant is a flat MUST NOT in RFC 9700 and is omitted from OAuth 2.1; it is not merely 'legacy but allowed'.

claims.text: RFC 9700, 'Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security', was published in January 2025 as BCP 240.
RFC 9700 updates RFC 6749, RFC 6750, and RFC 6819 rather than obsoleting them, extending their threat model and deprecating modes of operation deemed less secure or insecure.
RFC 9700 is the published successor to the long-running draft-ietf-oauth-security-topics series.
RFC 9700 requires that authorization servers MUST use exact string matching when comparing client redirection URIs against pre-registered redirect URIs.
The exact-matching rule carries a narrow carve-out for localhost/loopback redirect URIs used by native apps, whose port varies at runtime.
RFC 9700 states that public clients MUST use PKCE to prevent authorization code injection and misuse of authorization codes, while for confidential clients use of PKCE is RECOMMENDED.
The blanket 'PKCE for every client' mandate belongs to OAuth 2.1, not to RFC 9700, which distinguishes MUST for public clients from RECOMMENDED for confidential ones.

RFC 9700 notes the OpenID Connect nonce does not protect authorization codes of public clients, since an attacker can call the token endpoint directly with a stolen code, making PKCE the appropriate defence.
RFC 9700 requires clients to prevent CSRF against the redirection endpoint — requests arriving at the redirect URI that did not originate at the authorization server.
RFC 9700 states that one-time-use CSRF tokens carried in the state parameter and securely bound to the user agent MUST be used for CSRF protection.

RFC 9700 permits clients that have confirmed the authorization server supports PKCE to rely on PKCE's CSRF protection instead of state, and notes that in OpenID Connect flows the nonce parameter provides CSRF protection.

RFC 9700 states clients and authorization servers MUST NOT expose open redirectors — URLs that forward the browser to arbitrary URIs taken from a query parameter — since these enable exfiltration of codes and access tokens.
RFC 9700 identifies the Referer HTTP header as a leakage channel that can disclose the authorization request or response URI, from either the authorization server's or the client's pages.
RFC 9700 advises that the authorization endpoint and the page rendered from the authorization response SHOULD NOT include third-party resources or links to external sites.
RFC 9700 describes clickjacking against the consent screen as a malicious site loading the target authorization page in a transparent iframe over decoy buttons.

RFC 9700 defines mix-up attacks as arising when a client talks to two or more authorization servers and at least one is attacker-controlled, letting the attacker trick the client into sending a code or token issued by the honest server to the compromised one.
RFC 9207 defines the iss authorization response parameter, carrying the authorization server's issuer identifier explicitly, as a countermeasure to mix-up attacks.

RFC 9207 requires a supporting client to extract iss from the authorization response, form-urldecode it, and compare it by simple string comparison to the issuer identifier of the server it sent the request to, rejecting the response on mismatch.
RFC 9700 states clients MUST NOT pass access tokens in a URI query parameter in the manner described in Section 2.3 of RFC 6750.
RFC 9700 requires that refresh tokens for public clients MUST either be sender-constrained or use refresh token rotation (Section 4.14).
RFC 9700 Section 4.14.2 presents refresh token rotation as a detection-and-correction mechanism for refresh token theft rather than a prevention mechanism.
RFC 8252 (BCP 212) requires that OAuth authorization requests from native apps be made through an external user-agent, normally the system browser, not an embedded user-agent.

RFC 8252 defines an embedded user-agent as one hosted by the requesting app that shares its security domain, so the app can read cookie storage and inspect or modify page content — which is why webviews are disallowed.
RFC 8252 endorses the in-app browser tab, a browser instance rendered inside the host app that retains the browser's full security properties and authentication state.
RFC 8252 defines three redirect mechanisms: private-use URI scheme redirection, claimed 'https' scheme URI redirection, and loopback interface redirection.
RFC 8252 notes private-use URI schemes are weak because multiple apps can register the same scheme, leaving it indeterminate which app receives the code.

RFC 8252 specifies loopback redirect URIs of the form http://127.0.0.1:{port}/{path} for IPv4 and http://[::1]:{port}/{path} for IPv6, and requires the authorization server to allow any port to be specified at request time.

'OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications' is an IETF Internet-Draft with intended status Best Current Practice; as of 2026-07-27 the current revision is draft-ietf-oauth-browser-based-apps-27 and it is not yet an RFC.
The browser-based apps draft presents three architectural patterns in decreasing order of security: Backend-For-Frontend, Token-Mediating Backend, and Browser-Based OAuth Client.
In the Backend-For-Frontend pattern the browser app delegates all OAuth responsibilities to a backend and routes all resource requests through it, so tokens never reach JavaScript.
The browser-based apps draft warns that short access token lifetimes and refresh token rotation are ineffective against an active XSS attacker, who simply obtains a fresh, independent set of tokens.
The browser-based apps draft recommends that if a browser app cannot use a non-exportable key API, it should isolate the private key from XSS by holding it in a closure variable or a Service Worker.

RFC 9449 defines DPoP, an application-layer mechanism that sender-constrains access and refresh tokens by binding them to a client-held public key proven per request, independently of the client authentication method.
RFC 9449 positions DPoP for cases where transport-layer binding is unavailable or undesirable, explicitly naming the dynamically downloaded browser single-page application.

RFC 8705 defines mutual-TLS client authentication and certificate-bound access tokens, binding a token to the client's X.509 certificate so a protected resource can verify the presenter is the client the token was issued to.

RFC 8705 registers x5t#S256 as the JWT confirmation method for the X.509 certificate SHA-256 thumbprint, conveyed inside the cnf structure in tokens and introspection responses, and requires the protected resource to compare it against the client certificate used for the connection.

A practical selection rule: mTLS suits server-to-server and regulated back-end deployments with existing PKI; DPoP suits public clients, browser apps, and mobile apps that cannot present a client certificate.
A scope in OAuth 2.0 is the mechanism for limiting an application's access to a user's account, requested by the client and granted by the resource owner.
RFC 8707 says the authorization server SHOULD audience-restrict issued access tokens to the indicated resources, expressed as the aud claim in a JWT or in the introspection response.
RFC 9068 requires that every individual scope string in a JWT access token's scope claim have meaning for the resources named in its aud claim.

RFC 9126 defines the pushed authorization request endpoint, where a client pushes authorization request parameters to the server over a back channel and receives a request_uri to reference them at the authorization endpoint.

snippets.note: Authorization response carrying the RFC 9207 iss parameter; the client must string-compare it to the expected issuer before continuing.

snippets.code:
POST /token HTTP/1.1
Host: server.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=refresh_token&refresh_token=tGzv3JOkF0XG5Qx2TlKWIA&scope=read
snippets.note: Refresh request; under RFC 9700 a public client's refresh token must be rotated or sender-constrained, so the response should carry a new refresh_token.
RFC 8252 loopback redirect forms; the authorization server must accept any port at request time.

snippets.code:
POST /token HTTP/1.1
Host: server.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=client_credentials&resource=https%3A%2F%2Fapi.example.com%2Forders
snippets.note: RFC 8707 resource indicator; an absolute URI with no fragment, and the server audience-restricts the issued token to it.

pitfalls: Citing RFC 9700 as mandating PKCE for confidential clients overstates it — MUST is for public clients, RECOMMENDED for confidential ones; the universal mandate belongs to OAuth 2.1.
Dropping state is only safe once the client has actually confirmed the authorization server supports PKCE; RFC 9700 conditions the substitution on that check.
A state value that is not one-time-use and not bound to the user agent session provides no CSRF protection, however random it looks.
Receiving the iss parameter is not the defence — the defence is comparing it to the expected issuer and rejecting on mismatch.
'Exact string matching' means the whole URI, not just the origin; wildcard paths, wildcard subdomains, or extra query parameters reopen the open-redirector exfiltration path.
An open redirector anywhere on the client's own domain — not just on the OAuth endpoints — is enough to exfiltrate codes, so the audit scope is the whole site.
Including third-party scripts, analytics, or external links on the authorization or redirect landing page creates a Referer leak channel for codes and tokens.
Refresh token rotation without reuse detection is cosmetic; the value comes from treating presentation of a rotated-out token as evidence of theft and revoking the grant.
Treating rotation and short token lifetimes as an XSS defence for SPAs is a known error — an active in-page attacker just obtains fresh, independent tokens.
DPoP in the browser does not stop an attacker present during token issuance, since they can bind fresh tokens to their own key pair.
Using an embedded webview for the authorization request violates RFC 8252 and hands the host app access to the user's credentials, cookies, and page content.
Registering a private-use URI scheme without PKCE leaves a code interception hole, because any other installed app can claim the same scheme.
Hardcoding a fixed loopback port in a desktop client breaks when the port is taken; the spec expects an ephemeral port and requires the server to accept it.
Broad, coarse scopes make audience restriction meaningless; without resource indicators a token minted for one API is replayable at every other API trusting the same issuer.

claims.text: invalid_request means the request is missing a required parameter, includes an invalid parameter value, includes a parameter more than once, or is otherwise malformed.
invalid_client is the token endpoint error for failed client authentication; in practice it means a wrong client_id/client_secret pair or the wrong client authentication method.
invalid_grant means the supplied authorization grant or refresh token is invalid, expired, revoked, does not match the redirect URI used in the authorization request, or was issued to another client.
A PKCE failure surfaces as invalid_grant: the token endpoint returns invalid_grant when the transformed code_verifier does not equal the stored code_challenge.
invalid_grant is also what a client sees when it replays an already-redeemed authorization code or a rotated-out refresh token, so one code covers several very different root causes.

unauthorized_client means the authenticated client is not authorized to use this authorization grant type at the token endpoint, or not authorized to request a token by this method at the authorization endpoint.
invalid_scope means the requested scope is invalid, unknown, malformed, or exceeds the scope granted by the resource owner.
unsupported_grant_type means the authorization grant type is not supported by the authorization server.
redirect_uri_mismatch is not an error code registered in RFC 6749; providers commonly surface it as an invalid_request variant or a provider-specific string.

RFC 6749 requires the authorization server not to automatically redirect the user agent when the redirect URI is missing, invalid, or mismatched, which is why redirect URI failures appear as an error page rather than as a redirect carrying error=.

For invalid_client, if the client attempted to authenticate via the Authorization request header field, the authorization server MUST respond with HTTP 401 and include a WWW-Authenticate response header field matching the authentication scheme used by the client.
The token endpoint response is the primary debugging artifact: a JSON object whose error and error_description members carry the server's diagnosis.

Access tokens are opaque to clients by contract, but RFC 9068 defines a standard JWT profile, so where a provider issues JWT access tokens the header and claims can be base64url-decoded for inspection.
RFC 7662 token introspection is the standard server-side way to ask an authorization server whether a token is currently active and what scopes and authorization context it carries.
RFC 7662 introspection responses can themselves be returned as signed JWTs where stronger assurance is required.
A loopback redirect URI is the spec-sanctioned way to receive a real authorization response on a developer machine, since authorization servers must accept any port for loopback.

Fetching /.well-known/openid-configuration or the RFC 8414 authorization server metadata document is the correct first step when debugging an unfamiliar provider, since it returns the live endpoint URLs and advertised capabilities.
RFC 9728 lets a resource server return a WWW-Authenticate challenge carrying a resource_metadata URL, giving clients a discoverable path from a 401 to the resource's requirements.

RFC 9728 requires that when metadata was retrieved from a URL given in the WWW-Authenticate resource_metadata parameter, the resource value returned MUST be identical to the URL the client used to reach the resource server.
The authorization server MUST require the use of TLS for requests to both the authorization endpoint and the token endpoint.

RFC 9126 pushed authorization requests move the authorization parameters onto a back channel, which an authorization server implementer can use to keep request parameters off the front channel entirely.

snippets.note: Token endpoint error shape: error is machine-readable, error_description is for humans only.

snippets.code:
curl -s https://accounts.example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration \
  | jq '{issuer, authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint, userinfo_endpoint, jwks_uri}'
snippets.note: Discovery is the correct first debugging step; the issuer value must exactly match the URL used and the iss in issued ID Tokens.

snippets.code:
code_verifier=$(openssl rand -base64 96 | tr -d '\n=+/' | cut -c1-64)
code_challenge=$(printf '%s' "$code_verifier" \
  | openssl dgst -binary -sha256 \
  | openssl base64 | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '=')
snippets.note: Computing the S256 challenge from the shell — base64url(SHA256(ASCII(code_verifier))).

snippets.code:
POST /introspect HTTP/1.1
Host: server.example.com
Authorization: Basic czZCaGRSa3F0MzpnWDFmQmF0M2JW
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

token=mF_9.B5f-4.1JqM
snippets.note: Introspection; the response's active member is the authoritative liveness answer for an opaque token.
RFC 9728 challenge pointing the client at protected resource metadata.

pitfalls: invalid_grant is overloaded across expired code, replayed code, PKCE mismatch, revoked refresh token, and redirect URI mismatch at the token endpoint, so it cannot be diagnosed without server-side logs.

redirect_uri_mismatch is a provider-specific string, not an RFC 6749 error code, and it usually appears as a rendered error page rather than a redirect, because the server must not redirect to an unverified URI.
error_description is explicitly for humans — branching client logic on its text breaks the first time the provider rewords it.
Clients must persist a rotated refresh token on every refresh, or they lock themselves out on the next call.
Building an authorization server from scratch means owning consent UX, key rotation, revocation, and audit logging — the protocol is the small part.

claims.text: OpenID Connect 1.0 is a simple identity layer built on top of the OAuth 2.0 protocol; OAuth 2.0 alone conveys authorization, and OIDC adds a standardized, verifiable authentication event.

OIDC lets a Relying Party verify an end-user's identity by relying on an authentication performed by an OpenID Provider, and OIDC authentication flows are defined in terms of OAuth 2.0 authorization flows.
OIDC adds a new token type to OAuth 2.0, the id_token, which is a JSON Web Token carrying claims about the authentication of the end user plus any other claims the Relying Party requested.
The ID Token is scoped to a particular client through its aud (audience) and nonce claims.
OIDC requires the client to reject an ID Token that does not list it as a valid audience, or that contains additional audiences the client does not trust.
The ID Token iss claim is a case-sensitive https URL with scheme, host and optional port and path, and no query or fragment component.
The ID Token exp claim marks the time on or after which the token MUST NOT be accepted, and the current time MUST be before it.
The at_hash claim is the base64url encoding of the left-most half of the hash of the ASCII access_token value, using the hash algorithm implied by the ID Token's JOSE alg header.

The nonce is a string value that associates a client session with an ID Token and mitigates replay attacks, passed unmodified from the authorization request into the ID Token, and OIDC requires sufficient entropy to prevent guessing.
The openid scope value is what turns an OAuth 2.0 authorization request into an OpenID Connect authentication request.
The UserInfo endpoint is an OAuth 2.0 protected resource that returns claims about the authenticated end user when presented with an access token; its URL MUST use the https scheme.
An OpenID Provider supporting Discovery MUST publish a JSON document at the Issuer concatenated with /.well-known/openid-configuration, returned as 200 OK with content type application/json.

To prevent impersonation, a Relying Party MUST ensure the Issuer URL used for the configuration request exactly matches the issuer claim in the returned metadata, and that both exactly match the iss claim in ID Tokens from that provider.
OIDC Discovery uses a path-suffixed well-known URI specifically to support multiple issuers per host in multi-tenant hosting.

As of 2026-07-27, OAuth 2.1 remains an Internet-Draft and has not been published as an RFC; the current revision is draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1-15, issued around 2 March 2026 with an expiry of 3 September 2026 and an intended status of Standards Track.
OAuth 2.1 is scoped to replace and obsolete RFC 6749 (the core framework) and RFC 6750 (bearer token usage) once published.
OAuth 2.1 requires PKCE for the authorization code grant, whereas PKCE was a separate extension not required by the OAuth 2.0 core.
OAuth 2.1 does not specify the implicit grant (response_type=token) and does not specify the resource owner password credentials grant.
OAuth 2.1 requires exact string matching of redirect URIs, tightening a comparison rule that OAuth 2.0 left looser.
OAuth 2.1's bearer token usage omits the option of sending bearer tokens in the query string of a URI.
OAuth 2.1 is a consolidation effort: it folds the widely adopted OAuth 2.0 extensions and BCP guidance into a single simplified core document rather than inventing new protocol.
RFC 8693 defines OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange as an HTTP/JSON security token service, using the grant type urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange.
RFC 8693 distinguishes impersonation, where the acting party becomes indistinguishable from the subject, from delegation, where the acting party retains its own identity while acting for the subject.

draft-ietf-oauth-identity-chaining, 'OAuth Identity and Authorization Chaining Across Domains', defines a mechanism to preserve identity and authorization information across trust domains; as of 2026-07-27 it is at revision 12, Standards Track, and not yet an RFC.

RFC 9728, OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata, defines a metadata format a client or authorization server can use to learn how to interact with a protected resource, including supported scopes and how to present a token.
The Model Context Protocol authorization specification builds MCP's authorization model on OAuth 2.1, with a protected MCP server acting as an OAuth 2.1 resource server.
MCP adopts RFC 9728, requiring MCP servers to publish a protected resource metadata document at /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource.

MCP requires clients to implement PKCE and to verify PKCE support before proceeding, using the S256 code challenge method whenever technically capable, and to implement RFC 8707 resource indicators in both the authorization request and the token request.
MCP requires servers to validate that presented tokens were issued specifically for them, which is the specification's defence against the token passthrough anti-pattern.

MCP's security considerations describe confused-deputy attacks on MCP proxy servers that use static client IDs with dynamic client registration and skip per-client consent before forwarding authorization requests.

snippets.note: An OIDC authentication request is an OAuth authorization request plus the openid scope and a nonce (line-wrapped for reading).
Decoded ID Token payload; the client must reject it if aud omits its client_id, and must check exp and nonce.
The issuer in the metadata must exactly match the URL used and the iss claim in issued ID Tokens.

pitfalls: Describing OAuth 2.1 as a published standard is wrong as of 2026-07-27; it is still draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1-15, an Internet-Draft.

Using an OAuth access token as proof of authentication is the classic category error; only the ID Token carries a verifiable authentication event, and only when its signature, iss, aud, exp, and nonce are all validated.
Omitting the openid scope yields a plain OAuth response with no id_token, a common cause of 'the provider isn't returning an ID token' reports.

Token passthrough — a gateway or MCP server forwarding a client's token upstream, or accepting a token minted for someone else — is explicitly an anti-pattern; servers must verify the audience is themselves.
Sending the ID Token to an API as if it were an access token is the mirror-image mistake: it is scoped to the client, not to the resource server.
